description: Be An Earth System Trend Detective
summary:
LakePulse (“Lake Trend Detective”) analyzes 26 years of NASA data for Lake Simcoe, Ontario, to separate long-term environmental trends from seasonal and year-to-year variation.

- Measures trends using Sen’s slope, confidence intervals and the Mann–Kendall test.
- Identifies significant night-time surface warming of about **0.65°C per decade** from 2000–2025.
- Examines 18 environmental variables and tests pre-written hypotheses without confusing correlation with causation.
- Uses a fine-tuned NASA–IBM Prithvi-EO-2.0 model to map land cover at 30 m resolution.
- Establishes a foundation for investigating lake mixing, oxygen, nutrients, algal blooms, habitat and water quality.

In simple terms: LakePulse helps us see whether a lake is truly changing or simply experiencing normal ups and downs.
- Why it matters: A warmer lake surface can affect seasonal mixing, deep-water oxygen, nutrient movement, algae growth, water quality, wildlife habitat and the timing of the food web.
- Who it can help: Lake-monitoring teams, water and public-health agencies, watershed planners, researchers, students, and fisheries and ecosystem managers.
- How it can help: It provides an early warning signal and shows where more measurements—such as oxygen, nutrients, algae and water-depth temperatures—may be needed.
LakePulse does not claim that temperature has already caused these effects. It provides evidence, testable hypotheses and a foundation for future lake-health research.
details:
TL;DR

What we built: An interactive web application that turns long Earth-observation records into understandable lake-trend results.

Main finding: Lake Simcoe’s May–October night-time surface temperature rose about **0.65 °C per decade from 2000–2025** (95% CI 0.33–0.92; p < 0.001).

How it works: LakePulse controls for seasonality, applies Sen’s slope and the Mann–Kendall test, checks satellite overpass-time drift, and tests whether relationships remain after long-term trends are removed.

What is creative: It combines transparent hypothesis testing with a fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0 model that maps land cover at 30 m near shorelines and streams.

Who it can help: Lake-monitoring and water-quality teams, watershed planners, public-health agencies, researchers, students, and fisheries and ecosystem managers.

Why it matters: Temperature is an early diagnostic signal that can guide further investigation of lake mixing, deep-water oxygen, nutrients, algal-bloom risk, habitat and drinking-water quality.

What we do not claim: Correlations do not prove causation; MODIS measures the surface skin, not the water column; and LakePulse has not yet measured currents, oxygen, nutrients or blooms directly.

Details

Trend analysis: Users can explore monthly records and May–October annual means for 18 variables. For each eligible series, LakePulse reports Sen’s slope, a 95% confidence interval and a Mann–Kendall result in plain language. A clearly labelled synthetic “Practice Lake” helps students understand the method without mixing practice data with Lake Simcoe observations.

Lake Simcoe result: The strongest result is a night-time surface warming rate of 0.649 °C per decade from 2000–2025. We prioritize the night-time record because Terra’s daytime overpass shifted earlier during the study period. Ontario’s independent in-lake monitoring also reports surface warming, providing an external consistency check.

Candidate drivers. After removing straight-line trends, sunlight remains associated with lake temperature (r = 0.66). Air temperature (r = 0.90) and humidity (r = 0.58) are exploratory leads because they were not part of the written hypothesis. The expected haze pathway was not detected, while NO₂ served as a negative control: no direct relationship was expected or found.

Land-cover foundation. We fine-tuned the NASA–IBM–Jülich Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M model on 636 cloud-masked Sentinel-2 summer tiles. An entire watershed and adjacent shoreline were held out for evaluation. The selected model achieved mean IoU of 0.5145, compared with 0.4794 for a per-pixel baseline, and produces 30 m maps near shores and streams. Nine years are insufficient for a land-cover trend, and wetland performance remains weak.

Impact and next research. The project’s relevance extends beyond fisheries. It can help identify where measurements of temperature at depth, dissolved oxygen, nutrients, chlorophyll and cyanobacteria are most valuable. Warmer, more stable surface water can increase bloom risk when nutrients are available, but LakePulse has not shown that warming caused a specific Lake Simcoe water-quality outcome. The project establishes a credible signal, testable hypotheses and a workflow that can be extended to more lakes.

Technology. The analysis uses Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, xarray, Shapely and pyproj. Land-cover development used PyTorch/TerraTorch, MLflow and NVIDIA L4/A100 GPUs in Google Colab. The interface uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and D3 and is deployed with Docker/nginx on Google Cloud Run. NASA data were accessed through AppEEARS, GES DISC and LAADS DAAC; complementary sources include Ontario open data, the 2020 Land Cover of Canada map and Copernicus Sentinel-2 imagery.
